title: Pulse, meter, and rhythmic notation
description: Retain pulse, tempo, meter, time signatures, and basic note values.

cards.back: The steady tap (beat) under the music.
How fast the pulse moves, often marked in BPM (beats per minute).
The grouping of beats into bars (measures).

cards.front: What does a time signature like 4/4 or 3/4 tell you?
cards.back: The top number is how many beats per bar. The bottom number names which duration gets one beat (4 = quarter note). 4/4 = four quarter-note beats; 3/4 = three.

cards.front: In a time signature, what does the bottom number 4 mean?
cards.back: The quarter note gets one beat.

cards.front: In 4/4, how many beats are a whole, half, quarter, eighth, and sixteenth note?
What does a dot after a note do?
cards.back: It adds half of that note’s value. A dotted quarter = 1.5 quarters.

cards.front: How do you play a dotted quarter plus an eighth in 4/4?
cards.back: Hold 1½ beats, then play the remaining half beat (count 1  2 &).
It joins two notes of the same pitch into one sustained duration.

cards.front: What is the difference between a tie and a slur?
cards.back: A tie is same pitch, one sound (duration math). A slur connects different pitches — articulation, not duration math.

cards.front: How is rhythm related to pitch?
cards.back: Rhythm is independent of pitch. The same chord progression can use different meters and note values.

cards.front: Why is rhythmic notation useful even if you mostly read tab?
cards.back: Tab often hides duration. Note values let you communicate and practice rhythm precisely against a pulse.

cards.front: How do you count a bar of quarter, two eighths, quarter, quarter in 4/4?
In 4/4, on which beats do you attack half notes?
In 3/4, what must you not do when playing quarter notes?
cards.back: Do not insert a fourth beat. The bar is only three quarter-note beats.
